summary: Provides ABNF grammars equivalent to the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) encodings for common elements of ASN.1 types. Specifications that use GSER can use these as a convenience for implementors. It is informational and supports RFC 3641.

eli5.summary: Writing a grammar is like listing which word orders are allowed in a sentence. This gives ready-made grammar pieces so others writing text-based data formats do not have to write them again.

questions: how are asn.1 values written as text
how does gser encode a boolean
subtitle: Ready-made ABNF grammar for the text encodings of common ASN.1 types, to help people who do not know ASN.1.

tldr.problem: The Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER) give a readable text form for any ASN.1 value, but specifications that use GSER may want an equivalent ABNF grammar for implementors who do not know ASN.1.
tldr.mechanism: This document supplies ABNF rules for the GSER encodings of the ASN.1 built-in types, the restricted string types and some directory types common in LDAP and X.500.
tldr.outcome: The ABNF is only a convenience: if it disagrees with GSER, GSER is definitive.

facts.label: Authority
facts.value: GSER is definitive over this ABNF

today: RFC 3642 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It supports RFC 3641, which defines GSER itself.

sections.title: Purpose and Status of the ABNF
sections.content:
The Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER), defined in RFC 3641, give a human-readable text encoding for an ASN.1 value of any ASN.1 type. A specification that uses GSER may add a non-normative ABNF description of the encoding for one ASN.1 type, as a convenience for implementors who are unfamiliar with ASN.1.

This document supplies ABNF for the GSER encodings of ASN.1 types that commonly appear in LDAP or X.500 syntaxes, plus the ASN.1 built-in types. It does not replace or alter GSER. If the ABNF and GSER disagree, GSER is definitive.
sections.eli5: This is a helper sheet that spells out the rules for writing data as text. If the helper sheet and the official rulebook ever disagree, the official rulebook wins.

sections.title: Separators
sections.content:
Three small rules are shared by the grammars for SET and SEQUENCE types. sp is zero or more space characters, msp is one or more spaces, and sep is an optional comma.

The sep rule is used when every component of a SET or SEQUENCE is OPTIONAL or DEFAULT. It produces an empty string only when the character just before it is {, so only the first optional component actually present has no leading comma.
sections.eli5: Some tiny rules say where spaces and commas go between the items in a list, so a list never starts with a stray comma.

sections.title: Built-in ASN.1 Types
sections.content:
Section 4 gives a rule for each built-in type except the restricted character strings. A BIT STRING is written as bstring (for example binary digits between single quotes followed by B) or, when the bit count is a multiple of four, optionally as hstring (hex digits followed by H). A BOOLEAN is TRUE or FALSE, and NULL is NULL.

An INTEGER is 0, a positive number, or a minus sign and a positive number. An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is either dotted decimal or an object descriptor name, and the RFC warns that a descriptor name is potentially ambiguous and should be used with care. An OCTET STRING is hex digits, and if the digit count is odd the last four bits are assumed to be zero.

A REAL that is zero MUST be encoded as 0. Other values are PLUS-INFINITY, MINUS-INFINITY, a base 10 number with mantissa and exponent, or a braced sequence with mantissa, base (2 or 10) and exponent. The more complex types (CHARACTER STRING, EMBEDDED PDV and EXTERNAL) are written as braced lists of named components.
sections.eli5: Each kind of simple value has its own spelling: yes and no are written TRUE and FALSE, numbers are written with digits, and bytes are written as pairs of hex digits.

sections.title: Restricted String Types
sections.content:
Characters of a restricted character string type are always written as UTF-8 between double quotes. A double quote inside the string, where the character set allows one, is escaped by repeating it. Some string types first need translating into UTF-8.

Several types, including NumericString, PrintableString, VisibleString, IA5String, GeneralizedTime and UTCTime, are already compatible with UTF-8, so no translation is needed. BMPString (UCS-2) and UniversalString (UCS-4) are translated to UTF-8, as are TeletexString, VideotexString, GraphicString and GeneralString.

The time types have strictly defined formats. UTCTime has a two-digit year, month, day, hour and minute, then optional seconds and a zone. GeneralizedTime has a two-digit century and year, and the seconds field may be 60 to allow a leap second.
sections.eli5: Text values are put inside double quotes. If the text itself needs a quote mark, you write it twice so nobody gets confused about where the text ends.

sections.title: Directory ASN.1 Types
sections.content:
Section 6 covers selected types from LDAP and X.500. An AttributeType is encoded like an OBJECT IDENTIFIER. A DirectoryString is either a plain quoted string or a choice tagged with a name such as teletexString, printableString, bmpString, universalString or uTF8String, followed by a colon and the value.

Names are written as quoted LDAP strings. An RDNSequence (which is syntactically equivalent to DistinguishedName and LocalName) is first turned into a string using the distinguishedName rule of RFC 2253, then quoted with embedded double quotes repeated. A RelativeDistinguishedName is handled the same way using the name-component rule, and an ORAddress (an X.400 address) is derived under RFC 2156 and encoded as a quoted IA5 string.
sections.eli5: Names in a directory, like a mailing address for a person, are first written the usual way and then wrapped in quotes so they fit the same text rules as everything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document contains an alternative description of parts of GSER but does not change GSER. It points readers to the Security Considerations section of GSER for the full security implications of using the encoding.
sections.eli5: This is just a copy of some rules in another form, so for safety advice you should look at the original rulebook.
